title: Stack Mappings
description: Maps the indicator files found in a repository to the skills, agents, templates and candidate commands appropriate to it. This is the file that decides what a repository looks like to the orchestrator, which makes a wrong entry here a wrong assumption applied to everything downstream.

stacks.description: The known stacks. Order here is presentation order only — detection order is declared separately and is the one that matters.

id.description: Stable identifier, referenced by detectionOrder and recorded in a repository's generated context. Renaming one silently unmaps every repository already detected as it.

indicators.description: Evidence that a repository is this stack. An empty array marks a fallback that matches nothing and is only reachable as the last entry in detectionOrder.

file.description: Filename or glob that must exist, relative to the repository root.

directory.description: Directory that must exist. Weaker evidence than a file with a `contains` clause — a folder named Commands is a convention, not a dependency.

contains.description: Substring that must appear inside the matched file. This is what separates 'has a package.json' from 'actually depends on this framework', and it is the difference between a detection and a guess.

templates.description: Template families under templates/ that apply to this stack.

skills.description: Skills made available when this stack is detected. Each must name a folder under skills/.

agents.description: Agents relevant to this stack. Each must be a declared agent.

commands.description: Candidate commands per verb, in the order they should be attempted. These are candidates, not facts: verification-loop runs them and reports which one actually worked, because a build command asserted from a file pattern and never executed is exactly the kind of plausible-sounding claim the grounding contract exists to stop.

conventions.description: Observed conventions for this stack — naming, test layout, state management. Free-form keys because the interesting convention differs per ecosystem, and forcing a fixed vocabulary would mean recording the wrong fact in the right field.

forbiddenCommands.description: Commands that must never run from an agent context, typically state-mutating infrastructure operations. Declaring them here is documentation; the destructive-gate hook is what enforces it, and prose in a config file has never stopped anything.

forbiddenCommandsReason.description: Why those commands are forbidden, so the rule survives the person who wrote it.

detectionOrder.description: Stack ids in the order they are tested, and the order is load-bearing: it runs most-specific-first. A Next.js repository also declares a react dependency, so testing react first would classify every Next.js repository as plain React and silently lose its routing conventions and build commands. The same applies to a .NET CQRS project, which is also a .NET shared library by indicator. The last entry should be the catch-all, which is the only honest answer when nothing matched.

verifiedCommandsRule.description: What to do when no candidate command works — ask once, persist the answer in the consumer repo's context file, and never overwrite that section on regeneration. A one-time question that persists beats a permanent 'not detected'.
